title: Summarise each chunk by fixed steps
statement: Teach summarising as a fixed routine for each chunk: mark the key who or what, keep what matters, write one new short sentence, and check it against the marks.
example: A narrative version retells one to two paragraphs at a time with a Somebody-Wanted-But-So-Then frame.
detail: A reading course's review standard, drawing on IES videos on a gist routine and on summarising narrative texts in third grade, makes summarising a modelled routine with fixed steps, retold chunk by chunk and not only at the end (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/dimensions/D3-reading-architecture.md`, line 22). The expository version marks the most important who or what, keeps the important information and drops the rest, puts it into a new short sentence rather than a reworded paragraph, and checks that sentence against the marks. Without the steps a learner tends to copy one sentence or reword the whole paragraph, and a chunk whose gist can't be said signals a breakdown (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/teaching-moves/gist-summarizing-routine.md`).

evidence.quote: Summarizing is a modeled routine with fixed steps (mark who/what → keep-important/discard-unnecessary → synthesize in own words, not a reworded paragraph → check against the marks; or a 'Somebody-Wanted-But-So-Then' frame), retold per chunk not only at the end
it into your own words (a new short sentence, not a reworded paragraph)
retold one to two paragraphs at a time
a child who copies a sentence verbatim (no comprehension) or one who rewords the whole paragraph (no compression)
if you can't produce the gist of the chunk you just read, that is the breakdown signal

citations.ref: Teaching Summarizing with Narrative Texts in Third Grade, REL West video
